title: Engineered Maternal Cells and Selective Dosage Compensation in Trisomy 21: A Mechanistic Hypothesis
content: Postnatal intervention in the dynamic gene dosage of trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) has long faced a dual bottleneck. Autologous trisomic cells exhibit chromosomal introversion, nuclear lamina damage, premature senescence, and abnormal secretion of proinflammatory, mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA)-rich mitovesicles, compromising their suitability as a stable, long-term autologous manufacturing platform. Meanwhile, universal allogeneic extracellular vesicles (EVs), lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), and viral vectors commonly face accelerated blood clearance (ABC) or adaptive immune neutralization when administered repeatedly for chronic conditions. In nature, maternal microchimeric cells can cross the placenta, persist in offspring, and participate in maintaining tolerance to non-inherited maternal antigens (NIMAs). This biological precedent raises a central question that merits independent testing: could cells from healthy disomic mothers and their engineered vesicles open a new route to long-term dosage normalization in trisomy 21, combining secretory homeostasis with immune compatibility? To address this question, we propose T21-DoseSwitch, a candidate maternal-cell-based epigenetic dosage compensation research system (a working system name, not a finalized single protein). The framework separates four independently falsifiable modules: the feasibility of local engineered-protein regulation, maternal manufacturing and delivery, the comparative immune advantage of mother–offspring pairing, and chromosome-wide extension through XIST. Four quantitative and engineering criteria are established: 1. Define the limits of leveraging pre-existing tolerance and preserve a DNA-free manufacturing process. Conditional depletion experiments in vivo show that removal of viable LysM⁺CD11c⁺ maternal microchimeric cells disrupts NIMA tolerance. We therefore do not claim that acellular maternal EVs can induce tolerance de novo. Instead, we propose testing whether DNA-free engineered maternal tolerogenic monocyte-derived dendritic cells (tolDCs), or mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) with enhanced HLA-G/PD-L1, can reduce immune clearance during repeated administration in recipients with pre-existing tolerance confirmed by MLR–ELISPOT screening. 2. Clarify cargo–carrier immune incompatibility and restore the engineered-protein and de novo design research direction. Although an EV lipid membrane may shield cargo from extracellular pre-existing anti-Cas9 antibodies, it cannot prevent CD8⁺ T-cell clearance triggered by MHC class I presentation of bacterial protein after cellular entry. The original T21-DoseSwitch-P (dCas9–KRAB + gRNA) is retained as a T-cell-free in vitro benchmark (P1); a compact epigenetic-memory approach inspired by CHARM is presented as an independent candidate reference (P2). De novo design of novel sequence-specific DNA-binding proteins is identified as an open research question in its own right. 3. Unify the 21q population-genetic screening model and define its limits of applicability. In the approximately 88.5%–93.2% of cases attributable to maternal meiotic nondisjunction, the theoretical expected density of paternal-specific SNPs absent from maternal cells across euchromatic 21q (33.6 Mb) is 0.5π, corresponding to 2,192–3,068 strict SpCas9 NGG sites and near-100% arm-wide coverage under the neutral model. This could substantially reduce theoretical on-target risk in maternal producer cells under specific targeting conditions. However, coverage within a single-gene core promoter window of ±500 bp falls to 6.3%–8.7% at the arm-wide mean GC content of 41% (9.7%–13.4% in a hypothetical high-GC scenario of 60%). Meiosis II (MII) isodisomy introduces a maternal heterozygosity trap with an unconditional peak of 14.81% (the conditional risk in child-only 2:1 screening equals the allele frequency p). Pure MII isodisomy combined with a maternal recessive pathogenic variant imposes an explicit limit on sequence-dependent homolog selection. 4. Quantify the co-arrival ceiling for cis installation of XIST and its relationship to the hypothetical engineering range. Analysis of the joint probability P(A ∩ B) and sequential conditional events suggests that split delivery with two carriers is suited only to in vitro troubleshooting, whereas in vivo application would require progression toward single-particle co-encapsulation. At an assumed integration efficiency ηint = 30%, the ideal theoretical ceiling for single-dose XIST integration is also 30%, insufficient to cover the upper half of the hypothetical engineering discussion range of 30%–50% functionally disomic cells in key target organs. This distinction points to different roles for local non-integrating approaches and cumulative strategies.
